newsitem.title: USA: US black farmers protest over "unfair treatment".
newsitem.headline: US black farmers protest over "unfair treatment".

text.p: Two hundred black farmers marched in front of Agriculture Department headquarters Wednesday protesting that discrimination in the granting of loans had driven many of them from their fields.
"We need change. We need it today," John Boyd, president of the National Black Farmers Association (NBFA), told the rally. "Our voices will be heard at the last plantation."
Boyd said black farmers needed loan funds immediately from the department so they could meet planting-time expenses or "they won't be here next year, I can promise you that."

There are fewer than 20,000 black farmers out of about two million farmers in the United States. The NBFA says racism and illegal bias in Agriculture Department crop support and farm loan programs have driven many blacks from farming.

Only two complaints by blacks have been settled since last December when Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman ordered a halt to foreclosures if a civil rights violation was alleged. Boyd said this was an unacceptably poor record.

The farmers and Glickman were expected to speak later on Wednesday at a hearing organized by the Congressional Black Caucus. Representative Maxine Waters, a California Democrat who chairs the caucus, told the farmers, "Ladies and gentlemen, we are going to make things right."

In February, Glickman announced a campaign to fight racial bias at the department including speedy settling of complaints filed by minority farmers. Some 241 complaints were pending, most of them more than a year old, at that point.

In a memorandum distributed to employees shortly before the rally, Glickman said all civil rights complaints, whether from farmers or agency employees, would be settled by June 6. The two "major financial settlements" with farmers over loan discrimination "underscore my commitment that USDA stands ready to resolve, quickly and fairly, legitimate civil rights complaints," he wrote.

Glickman also pointed to regulations issued this week to freeze the loan foreclosure process as soon as a civil rights complaint is filed. In the past, only foreclosure sales were halted by such a complaint.
Legislation was being drafted to carry out several reforms including a federal takeover of 12,000 county employees who run the local Agriculture Department offices, he said.
